I don’t need any influencer to lobby me, all I need to do is just to do the will and the wish of the people. Is it the policy of the state government now that your roads will be concrete pavement? We are not only just doing the concrete pavement, one of the reasons we are doing it is because of the swampy nature of many of our areas. We are in the rainforest zone and we need to sustain the roads. We have carefully studied to see that without concrete pavement, we will have problems within a short time. We are preparing for the future so that by the time when this government leaves, the next government will come and concentrate on other areas so that development will spread. Look, we are not only working on infrastructure, we are also working on security. We are trying to make Edo very safe, safer than we met it. When we came in, within a week I recorded about 11 people dead not in an accident, somebody will get into a shop and kill the person there, somebody will just see someone on the road and shoot him. Why? The killers were cultists. I remember when the BBC guys came here and asked: Do you fear them? I said “I don’t fear because I am working for the people and I want to save Edo people”. Today, you can hardly hear somebody die as a result of cult issues because we took a stiff measure that when you kill, we go to your family house or your personal house or wherever you live, whether you left your hotel to that place, I will demolish that hotel. If you leave your father’s house to that place to kill, I will demolish your father’s house. So these are stiff measures we have taken that are really working for us and, to be honest with you, if not that we have done that, maybe you won’t be able to stay in Benin for two nights. Today nightlife is back, business is booming at night, even supermarkets are beginning to open at night; in the next few weeks, it will be safer such that everywhere, at every corner of the state, there will be the police to watch everyone. They will be equipped even with motorbikes so that when somebody thinks he can run, then they will follow the person. Whether you take a bush path, they will follow you up. So we are prepared to secure the city. We are prepared to secure the state. Are you ready for state police? Yes, we are prepared. We were one of the first states to pass the bill; when others were talking, we said no, it is working for us and, right now, to be honest with you, even with our vigilantes, we already have state police because it is working for us. Edo is safe. Remember there was this kidnapping that happened and within 24 hours which has never happened in Nigeria, we got the guys, so that is it. We are even prepared to go to other states when they take any of our citizens. We did it in Kogi, then something happened in Ogun, I called the governor, I said, “Please, I don’t want my person to stay with this kidnapper for more than five days”, and, as God would have it, he was able to get them out within a short time. So somebody has to be prudent with everything. How are you managing the burden of debt servicing versus project implementation in the state? Many times when I say I am rooting for Mr. President’s 2.5 million votes, people wonder why I am saying this. It is because of the evidence of what we are seeing today. The FAAC allocation has increased and our own internally generated revenue has also increased. So what we are doing is prudent spending. We focus on things that matter to the people and we are not interested in ourselves, so what matters to the people is what we spend money on. Is there any plan to float an airline considering the traffic coming in and out of the state? We are already on it. If you look at the newspapers a few days ago, there was widespread publication on Edo Air; so, very soon, you will see it. There is the challenge of gully erosion in several places in the state. What is your government doing about this? We have actually set up an ecological agency to handle such cases. We have to do our best to see who will secure our place for the teachers. You recently employed some teachers, but there is still shortage of teachers in several schools. What are you doing about this? We are still going to hire more teachers to be honest with you, because when we were growing up, if there were no teachers, we wouldn’t be where we are today. So, the education for the children is very key and that is one of the reasons when I came in I was so interested to see that we fixed our educational system. There was EdoBEST but it was EdoBEST for Obaseki and not for Edo people. That is the truth and they just used that to take away Edo money because when I looked at the system called EdoBEST based on what I saw, it was just like a tablet and, first of all, before you could even use the tablet, there should be internet which is 3 or 4 5G but maybe the children were just buying little airtime and load on their phones to operate it. And the curriculum they were using was actually not our own curriculum. It was Kenya and I frowned at it and so I stopped it and some governors that were convinced to do it but didn’t know what it was all about now got in touch with me and asked me how I got out of it. In Edo, we are concentrating on a school access programme and, for me, that is the way to go because, first of all, you need classrooms for the children. They should have at least water in school, they should have toilets and they should also have teachers. So once you have all these on ground children want to go there. Now in Edo State, many children don’t want to go to private schools, they want to come into government schools because the basic amenities for them are being provided and teachers are also there. What is the situation of those recently sentenced to death for kidnapping? I pray our brothers are not involved in kidnapping because I will sign the death warrant, even if it is my father, I will sign it. The truth is this, we just have to get some bad elements out of the system for the system to stand, and these people

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 22 – Swirls and Colors on Jupiter from Juno
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 22 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Swirls and Colors on Jupiter from Juno Explanation: What creates the colors in Jupiter’s clouds? No one is sure. The thick atmosphere of Jupiter is mostly hydrogen and helium , elements which are colorless at the low temperatures of the Jovian cloud tops . Which trace molecules provide the colors remains a topic of research , although small amounts of ammonium hydrosulfide are one leading candidate . What is clear from the featured color-enhanced image — and many similar images — is that lighter clouds are typically higher up than darker ones. Pictured, light clouds swirl around reddish regions toward the lower right, while they appear to cover over some darker domains on the upper right. The featured image was taken by the robotic Juno spacecraft in 2018 during its 14th low pass over Jupiter . Juno continues in its looping elliptical orbit, swooping near the huge planet every 33 days and exploring a slightly different sector each time around. The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung. item.title: Trouble in House of God: Single-founder churches spark succession storm
item.description: By Ebunoluwa Sessou & Nnamdi Ojiego The leadership dispute at the Fountain of Life Church, Lagos, following the death of its founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, has brought a difficult question facing many founder-led churches into public focus: Who takes charge when the person around whom a ministry was built is no longer there? The disagreement over the position of his son, Pastor Jimmy Odukoya, has moved from the church’s internal leadership structure to the courts, with competing claims over the late founder’s wishes, the church’s constitution and the authority of its Board of Trustees. On November 17, a faction of the church’s trustees announced that Jimmy was no longer recognised as senior pastor. The trustees said their decision followed a review of the church’s succession arrangements and a video recording made by the late Taiwo Odukoya in December 2021, in which he allegedly named Pastor Kunle Areogun as his preferred successor. Odukoya’s wife, Pastor Bimbo, a co-founder of the church, had earlier died in a plane crash. According to the trustees, the late founder proposed that Jimmy serve as Areogun’s administrative assistant and head of the church’s youth ministry. They said the recording was made available to them in December 2025 and was not presented when Jimmy was appointed senior pastor in September 2023. The trustees subsequently named Pastor Rotimi Okpaise as interim spiritual and administrative leader, pending consultations and the establishment of a substantive leadership structure. Controversy over remarriage The dispute came on the heels of Jimmy’s recent remarriage, which the trustees identified as one of their concerns about his continued leadership of the church. Jimmy introduced his new wife, Mo Jasyme, to the congregation during a Sunday service on November 1, 2026, describing her as his wife and the church’s new first lady. The union was publicly blessed by Pastor Tunde Bakare, founder of the Citadel Global Community Church, who prayed for the couple during the service. The marriage followed the end of Jimmy’s previous union with Oluwakemi Banjoko, whom he married in London in March 2013. The couple have two children. The circumstances surrounding the breakdown of that marriage have not been publicly established. During the introduction of his new wife, Jimmy said his first marriage had ended before he became senior pastor in September 2023. The trustees, however, described the remarriage and its public blessing as contrary to the church’s teachings, the values of its founders and the standards expected of its spiritual leadership. They said the development had caused distress among members and brought the church into public controversy and disrepute. Their statement placed the marriage alongside the disagreement over the succession recording as grounds for their action against him. item.dc:creator: Oboh
item.content:encoded: By Ebunoluwa Sessou & Nnamdi Ojiego The leadership dispute at the Fountain of Life Church, Lagos, following the death of its founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, has brought a difficult question facing many founder-led churches into public focus: Who takes charge when the person around whom a ministry was built is no longer there? The disagreement over the position of his son, Pastor Jimmy Odukoya, has moved from the church’s internal leadership structure to the courts, with competing claims over the late founder’s wishes, the church’s constitution and the authority of its Board of Trustees. On November 17, a faction of the church’s trustees announced that Jimmy was no longer recognised as senior pastor. The trustees said their decision followed a review of the church’s succession arrangements and a video recording made by the late Taiwo Odukoya in December 2021, in which he allegedly named Pastor Kunle Areogun as his preferred successor. Odukoya’s wife, Pastor Bimbo, a co-founder of the church, had earlier died in a plane crash. According to the trustees, the late founder proposed that Jimmy serve as Areogun’s administrative assistant and head of the church’s youth ministry. They said the recording was made available to them in December 2025 and was not presented when Jimmy was appointed senior pastor in September 2023. The trustees subsequently named Pastor Rotimi Okpaise as interim spiritual and administrative leader, pending consultations and the establishment of a substantive leadership structure. Controversy over remarriage The dispute came on the heels of Jimmy’s recent remarriage, which the trustees identified as one of their concerns about his continued leadership of the church. Jimmy introduced his new wife, Mo Jasyme, to the congregation during a Sunday service on November 1, 2026, describing her as his wife and the church’s new first lady. The union was publicly blessed by Pastor Tunde Bakare, founder of the Citadel Global Community Church, who prayed for the couple during the service. The marriage followed the end of Jimmy’s previous union with Oluwakemi Banjoko, whom he married in London in March 2013. The couple have two children. The circumstances surrounding the breakdown of that marriage have not been publicly established. During the introduction of his new wife, Jimmy said his first marriage had ended before he became senior pastor in September 2023. The trustees, however, described the remarriage and its public blessing as contrary to the church’s teachings, the values of its founders and the standards expected of its spiritual leadership. They said the development had caused distress among members and brought the church into public controversy and disrepute. Their statement placed the marriage alongside the disagreement over the succession recording as grounds for their action against him. The trustees subsequently named Pastor Rotimi Okpaise as interim spiritual and administrative leader, pending consultations and the establishment of a substantive leadership structure. Jimmy and the church’s opposing leadership position rejected the announcement, insisting that his appointment in September 2023 was unanimously approved by the Board of Trustees and that those who announced his removal lacked the constitutional authority to do so. The disagreement escalated when the Lagos State High Court, on Wednesday issued an interim order restraining Jimmy from presenting himself as the church’s senior pastor and spiritual head, and from interfering with its governance and activities. The order was made ex parte while the case was adjourned until December 1. Sealed Meanwhile, the church, on Friday, dismissed reports that its premises had been sealed and announced that its regular Sunday service would hold at 9am, although its 2026 Thanksgiving Service had been postponed. At the centre of the dispute are questions that extend beyond the personalities involved. How should a church founded and led by one individual determine who succeeds that person? Does a founder’s recorded preference override a later appointment made under the church’s constitution? What role should family members, trustees, elders and other senior ministers play? And how can a ministry preserve its identity while ensuring that leadership is transferred through a process accepted by its members? For churches whose growth, public identity and authority have been closely associated with their founders, succession can involve spiritual, administrative, legal and family considerations. Pattern The experiences of other Nigerian churches show that there is no single pattern. The Church of God Mission International, founded by Archbishop Benson Idahosa, offers an example of a founder’s widow taking over leadership. Following his death in March 1998, his wife, Margaret Idahosa, succeeded him as presiding bishop. She had been actively involved in the ministry before his death. Their son, Bishop Faith Benson Idahosa, has also held leadership positions within the church’s institutions. The transition at the Synagogue Church of All Nations (SCOAN) also brought a founder’s widow to the forefront. After the death of Prophet T.B. Joshua in June 2021, his wife, Evelyn Joshua, emerged as the church’s leader. The transition attracted public attention amid reports of disagreements over the church’s future. The church denied that there was a succession battle and said it would follow its founder’s instructions. In September 2021, the Federal High Court in Lagos affirmed Evelyn Joshua as a trustee of SCOAN after a petition to fill the vacancy created by her husband’s death. A similar family transition occurred at New Anointing Ministries in Makurdi, founded by the late Rev. Godwin Ikyernum. Following his death in an automobile accident in March 1997, his wife, Hannah Ikyernum, assumed leadership. The ministry is now led by their son, Pastor Joshua Ikyernum. Accounts of the transition have also documented dissatisfaction among some of the founder’s former associates, with some reportedly leaving the ministry. Succession without spouses, children as beneficiaries Other churches have followed succession arrangements that did not depend on a founder’s spouse or children. The leadership of the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG), founded by the late Rev. Josiah Akindayomi, passed to Pastor Enoch Adeboye in 1981. The church’s account of the transition says Akindayomi communicated his choice of successor in a sealed pronouncement that was read after his burial. Adeboye, who was not the founder’s biological son, subsequently became General Overseer. At the Foursquare Gospel Church in Nigeria, leadership has also changed through an electoral process. In July 2019, delegates elected Rev. Sam Aboyeji as the church’s fifth General Overseer, succeeding Rev. Felix Meduoye, who had completed an eight-year tenure. Aboyeji emerged through a contest involving other candidates, including Rev. Isaac Komolafe. The Upper Room Baptist Church provides another example of an institutionally managed transition. The church, which began in 1987 with 17 founding families, operates a governance structure involving a General Council, Trustees and a General Assembly. Pastor Oluleke Akinola succeeded its first General Overseer, Pastor Abiodun Longe, in 2004. After 21 years in office, Akinola handed over to Pastor Rufus Dada on December 31, 2024. The Apostolic Church Nigeria also experienced a leadership transition through an election in February 2025, when Pastor Lawrence Oladele emerged as National Leader. These examples illustrate the range of arrangements available to churches: Succession by a spouse or child, appointment of a designated successor, election by delegates and leadership transitions managed through established institutional structures. item.title: 55 Days to Polls: Opposition parties, APC at war over political attacks
item.description: •Stakeholders warn of threat to democracy, ask candidates to rein in supporters By Henry Umoru, John Alechenu, Luminous Jannamike & Deola Badru In the build up to the 2027 general elections increasingly characterised by attacks on supporters of political parties, destruction of campaign materials, intimidation and allegations of political thuggery, opposition parties and the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, have traded accusations over who is responsible for the growing violence. The political atmosphere across the country 55 days to the polls is becoming increasingly charged, with fears that the situation could deteriorate further in the coming days if political leaders fail to rein in their supporters and caution their members against inflammatory statements and actions. The APC had accused opposition parties of sponsoring violence and hiring thugs to disrupt political activities, particularly following the incident involving President Bola Tinubu during his visit to a mosque in Abuja for prayers. Sponsoring violence It claimed the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) are sponsoring violence, spreading misinformation and recruiting young Nigerians to disrupt its presidential campaign activities ahead of the 2027 general elections. Dr Dele Alake, spokesperson for the APC Presidential Campaign Council, made the allegations in a statement against the backdrop of recent attacks and confrontations involving political parties and their supporters nationwide. The statement came days after suspected political thugs disrupted an NDC town hall meeting in Ikeja, Lagos, on November 12, where the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, was expected to address supporters. “To create the false narrative of citizens’ discontent against the President, the ADC and NDC now sponsor hoodlums, arm them with cudgels and banners, and commandeer them to chant ‘Bamaiyi’ at APC campaign rallies,” the statement said. “The latest instance of this abhorrent and anti-democratic stunt was the desecration of an Abuja Mosque last Friday, where these thugs were mobilised to pelt the presidential motorcade with stones. “Also concerning is how our party’s campaign billboards are being destroyed under cover of night by opposition-sponsored agents. This is unacceptable and antithetical to democratic ideals,” the campaign council added. “Again, we call on the ADC and NDC leaders to stop the dangerous conscription of ignorant young Nigerians for unwholesome political activities that put their lives at risk, while those leaders’ own children luxuriate in splendour abroad”. item.dc:creator: Oboh
item.content:encoded: •Stakeholders warn of threat to democracy, ask candidates to rein in supporters By Henry Umoru, John Alechenu, Luminous Jannamike & Deola Badru In the build up to the 2027 general elections increasingly characterised by attacks on supporters of political parties, destruction of campaign materials, intimidation and allegations of political thuggery, opposition parties and the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, have traded accusations over who is responsible for the growing violence. The political atmosphere across the country 55 days to the polls is becoming increasingly charged, with fears that the situation could deteriorate further in the coming days if political leaders fail to rein in their supporters and caution their members against inflammatory statements and actions. The APC had accused opposition parties of sponsoring violence and hiring thugs to disrupt political activities, particularly following the incident involving President Bola Tinubu during his visit to a mosque in Abuja for prayers. Sponsoring violence It claimed the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) are sponsoring violence, spreading misinformation and recruiting young Nigerians to disrupt its presidential campaign activities ahead of the 2027 general elections. Dr Dele Alake, spokesperson for the APC Presidential Campaign Council, made the allegations in a statement against the backdrop of recent attacks and confrontations involving political parties and their supporters nationwide. The statement came days after suspected political thugs disrupted an NDC town hall meeting in Ikeja, Lagos, on November 12, where the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, was expected to address supporters. “To create the false narrative of citizens’ discontent against the President, the ADC and NDC now sponsor hoodlums, arm them with cudgels and banners, and commandeer them to chant ‘Bamaiyi’ at APC campaign rallies,” the statement said. “The latest instance of this abhorrent and anti-democratic stunt was the desecration of an Abuja Mosque last Friday, where these thugs were mobilised to pelt the presidential motorcade with stones. “Also concerning is how our party’s campaign billboards are being destroyed under cover of night by opposition-sponsored agents. This is unacceptable and antithetical to democratic ideals,” the campaign council added. “Again, we call on the ADC and NDC leaders to stop the dangerous conscription of ignorant young Nigerians for unwholesome political activities that put their lives at risk, while those leaders’ own children luxuriate in splendour abroad”. Violence However, opposition parties, including the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC; Social Democratic Party, SDP; New Nigeria Peoples Party, NNPP; Action Democratic Party, ADP; Peoples Democratic Party, PDP; African Democratic Congress, ADC; and Labour Party, LP, in chats with Sunday Vanguard, have rejected the allegations, with some accusing the ruling party of encouraging violence through its rhetoric and actions. While some parties have urged President Tinubu to call APC governors and other party chieftains to order, others have warned that reckless political statements, poverty, hunger and intolerance among political leaders are worsening the situation. The National Publicity Secretary of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Osa Director, said the ruling party was looking for scapegoats rather than accepting responsibility for the atmosphere of violence allegedly created by its members. Director said: “The APC led by President Tinubu said all is fair in politics. The APC members across the country saw this as a clarion call to arms. Evidence abound everywhere about their rhetoric of violence. Why turn around to blame the opposition parties. We think and know that the APC is clueless and rudderless, therefore they are looking for scapegoat to blame for their monumental failures. “The NDC will continue to explore all legal and constitutional means to carry out its campaigns. Those who engage in violence are those who have nothing to campaign with.” Threats to democracy Similarly, the Social Democratic Party, SDP, described political violence as a serious threat to democracy, insisting that political actors must embrace peaceful campaigns and respect the rule of law. The National Publicity Secretary of the SDP and Chairman, Media and Publicity Committee of the party’s National Campaign Council, Araba Rufus Aiyenigba, said political violence, whether during campaigns or at any other stage of the electoral process, was unacceptable. He said: “Political violence during campaigns or in any form in the course of the electoral processes is highly condemnable and is considered a threat to democracy. “Every Nigerian owes it a duty to the true interest of the nation and the good of our polity, to strongly promote and champion violence-free politicking and elections. “As a nation, irrespective of tribe, religion, and region, we all gain more when an atmosphere of peace is engendered in our democracy and order pervades our political landscapes. “The SDP is a frontline political party that prioritises discipline and code of conduct in our political operations and activities. We are reputed to have always been at the forefront of the promotion of the rule of law, as evident in the plethora of legal cases we have pursued and won, rather than treading the ignoble path of inciting violence or promoting breakdown of law and order. “The SDP is acclaimed as a national political party that thrives on the supremacy of nationalistic ideas over the strength of might and the brute force to snatch power. “Our campaigns have always been conducted on the higher pedestal of civilised and democratic orientation that thrives on winning power by the free will of the people, social justice, and not jungle justice.” Intimidation Aiyenigba called for stiffer sanctions against political actors and parties found promoting violence, warning that Nigerians must be allowed to exercise their democratic rights without intimidation. “The SDP, therefore, calls for strong legislations and stiff sanctions against every political actor or any political party found to promote violence in whatever form. “Our democracy must be truly democratic in form and practice. Nigerian people must have the freedom to exercise their fundamental rights, free of any form of intimidation or harassment. “That is what guarantees the survival of our democracy and enhances national stability, particularly as we enter the 2027 general elections,” he said. Intolerance For the New Nigeria Peoples Party, NNPP, the growing violence is partly a consequence of intolerance among political leaders and the worsening economic situation in the country. The National Chairman of the party, Dr Agbo Major, said political parties must exercise restraint, particularly at a time when the country was already divided along ethnic and religious lines. Major said: “It’s an unfortunate situation but we can only insist that the political parties exercise restraint. We are at trying moments dangerously divided along ethnic and religious lines. ‘Political leaders must be careful’ “The so-called bigger political parties must be careful and desist from encouraging violence. My party, the New Nigeria Peoples Party is for peaceful election. “Violence is increasing due to intolerance from political leaders and the large scale poverty that is on the increase on daily basis. The people are angry, there is hunger everywhere. “We are aggressively talking to our members to be peaceful and orderly as the election activities unfold. We must have a country that we will call ours.” Also blaming the ruling party for the worsening political atmosphere, the Action Democratic Party, ADP, said the APC must accept responsibility for the consequences of its political rhetoric and alleged misuse of public resources. item.title: ABBACARE: How Kano is expanding healthcare access for the most vulnerable
item.description: By Hassan A. Karofi Access to affordable healthcare remains a major challenge for millions of Nigerians, particularly low-income households and vulnerable groups who often delay or forgo treatment because of the cost. In Kano State, the ABBACARE Initiative is one of the interventions aimed at addressing this challenge through social health insurance. Implemented by the Kano State Contributory Healthcare Management Agency (KSCHMA), ABBACARE is designed to provide healthcare coverage for vulnerable groups, including pregnant women, persons living with sickle cell disorder and emergency patients. Its focus is on reducing the financial barriers that prevent people from accessing essential medical services. According to figures provided for the initiative, ABBACARE has enrolled 28,721 beneficiaries and extended service delivery to 13 hospitals across Kano State’s three senatorial zones. These figures point to an effort to widen access to healthcare, although the programme’s long-term impact will depend on the quality of services available, the regularity of funding and the ability to sustain coverage as more people are enrolled. The initiative also highlights the role state governments can play in advancing Universal Health Coverage through social health insurance. While national policies provide an important framework, state-level programmes such as ABBACARE can help address local healthcare needs and extend financial protection to people who might otherwise struggle to pay for treatment. The programme is part of a wider set of health interventions under Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf’s administration. Another is the Gida-Gida Lafiya Project, which focuses on hypertension and other non-communicable diseases through the distribution of customised digital blood pressure monitors. The devices are intended to help beneficiaries monitor their blood pressure, identify possible health risks early and seek medical attention when necessary. Their adaptation to provide guidance in local languages also reflects the importance of making health information accessible to people in their communities. Although ABBACARE and Gida-Gida Lafiya address different aspects of healthcare, they speak to two related challenges. The former seeks to reduce the financial burden of accessing treatment, while the latter encourages prevention, regular monitoring and early intervention. Both approaches are relevant in a health system where the cost of treatment and late presentation at hospitals can worsen health outcomes. However, the success of such interventions should not be measured by enrolment figures or the number of devices distributed alone. Their value will ultimately depend on whether beneficiaries can consistently access the services promised, whether participating hospitals have the capacity to provide quality care and whether the programmes are adequately funded over time. The Kano State Ministry of Health and the leadership of KSCHMA therefore have important roles to play
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Okogba
item.content:encoded: By Hassan A. Karofi Access to affordable healthcare remains a major challenge for millions of Nigerians, particularly low-income households and vulnerable groups who often delay or forgo treatment because of the cost. In Kano State, the ABBACARE Initiative is one of the interventions aimed at addressing this challenge through social health insurance. Implemented by the Kano State Contributory Healthcare Management Agency (KSCHMA), ABBACARE is designed to provide healthcare coverage for vulnerable groups, including pregnant women, persons living with sickle cell disorder and emergency patients. Its focus is on reducing the financial barriers that prevent people from accessing essential medical services. According to figures provided for the initiative, ABBACARE has enrolled 28,721 beneficiaries and extended service delivery to 13 hospitals across Kano State’s three senatorial zones. These figures point to an effort to widen access to healthcare, although the programme’s long-term impact will depend on the quality of services available, the regularity of funding and the ability to sustain coverage as more people are enrolled. The initiative also highlights the role state governments can play in advancing Universal Health Coverage through social health insurance. While national policies provide an important framework, state-level programmes such as ABBACARE can help address local healthcare needs and extend financial protection to people who might otherwise struggle to pay for treatment. The programme is part of a wider set of health interventions under Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf’s administration. Another is the Gida-Gida Lafiya Project, which focuses on hypertension and other non-communicable diseases through the distribution of customised digital blood pressure monitors. The devices are intended to help beneficiaries monitor their blood pressure, identify possible health risks early and seek medical attention when necessary. Their adaptation to provide guidance in local languages also reflects the importance of making health information accessible to people in their communities. Although ABBACARE and Gida-Gida Lafiya address different aspects of healthcare, they speak to two related challenges. The former seeks to reduce the financial burden of accessing treatment, while the latter encourages prevention, regular monitoring and early intervention. Both approaches are relevant in a health system where the cost of treatment and late presentation at hospitals can worsen health outcomes. However, the success of such interventions should not be measured by enrolment figures or the number of devices distributed alone. Their value will ultimately depend on whether beneficiaries can consistently access the services promised, whether participating hospitals have the capacity to provide quality care and whether the programmes are adequately funded over time. The Kano State Ministry of Health and the leadership of KSCHMA therefore have important roles to play in ensuring that the initiatives deliver their intended benefits. Dr Rahila Mukhtar, whose role in the agency’s operations and healthcare financing efforts has been noteworthy, is among the key figures associated with the implementation of approaches such as ABBACARE. The agency’s work in administering the initiative underscores the importance of effective health insurance management. Enrolling vulnerable people is an important first step, but maintaining reliable access to care requires proper coordination with healthcare providers, transparent management of funds, regular monitoring and accountability to beneficiaries. For Kano, the next task is to consolidate the gains made through ABBACARE and ensure that the programme remains accessible and sustainable. Expanding coverage will also require attention to the capacity of participating hospitals and the experiences of beneficiaries, particularly those who depend on the scheme for maternal care, treatment of sickle cell disorder and emergency services. Other states can draw useful lessons from Kano’s experience, especially in using social health insurance to protect vulnerable populations. However, the model’s wider relevance will depend on evidence of its outcomes, affordability and sustainability. As Nigeria pursues Universal Health Coverage, initiatives such as ABBACARE show why state-level action matters. The real measure of progress will not simply be the number of people enrolled, but whether they can obtain timely, affordable and quality healthcare when they need it. •Karofi writes from Abuja and can be reached at hassankarofi@gmail.com. item.title: ASIWAJU: Why I support 2nd term for President Tinubu
item.description: By Moriamoh Ojikutu A friend asked me recently, “Do you think Asiwaju is working?” My answer was simple: “Yes. He is doing his job.” Let me be clear about where I stand. I strongly support President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and his administration, and I want him re-elected for a second term. I believe in his leadership and the direction of his administration. I want him to complete the work he has started and deliver the lasting improvements I believe are possible. That does not mean I think everything is perfect. It certainly does not mean I am unaware of the difficulties Nigerians are facing. I live here. I run businesses here. I employ people, pay bills, buy fuel and deal with rising costs. I know what it means to reconsider spending, adjust plans and keep going when doing business becomes more difficult. My support exists alongside that reality, not outside it. When I say he is doing his job, I mean that I believe he is confronting difficult problems rather than leaving them for someone else. But taking difficult decisions is not the finish line. Delivering results that Nigerians can see, touch and feel is. Reform Is Rarely Comfortable: I do not believe Nigeria’s economic difficulties began with this administration, nor do I believe every problem can be resolved within a few years. My view is that some difficult decisions had been postponed for too long. President Tinubu’s administration has pursued major changes, including the removal of petrol subsidies and reforms to the foreign exchange system. I support the decision to confront those structural problems. But I also recognise the hardship Nigerians have experienced during this period. Families are making difficult choices. Businesses are adjusting their operations. People are working hard and still worrying about what they can afford. Those experiences deserve to be heard, not dismissed with political slogans. For me, acknowledging the pain does not mean rejecting the need for reform. It means asking how reform can be implemented more effectively and how people can be better protected through the transition. A policy can have a sound objective and still need adjustments. I know what it means to reconsider spending, adjust plans and keep going when doing business becomes more difficult. My support exists alongside that reality, not outside it. When I say he is doing his job, I mean that I believe he is confronting difficult problems rather than leaving them for someone else. But taking difficult decisions is not the finish line. Delivering results that Nigerians can see, touch and feel is. Reform Is Rarely Comfortable: I do not believe Nigeria’s economic difficulties began with this administration, nor do I believe every problem can be resolved within a few years. My view is that some difficult decisions had been postponed for too long. President Tinubu’s administration has pursued major changes, including the removal of petrol subsidies and reforms to the foreign exchange system. I support the decision to confront those structural problems. But I also recognise the hardship Nigerians have experienced during this period. Families are making difficult choices. Businesses are adjusting their operations. People are working hard and still worrying about what they can afford. Those experiences deserve to be heard, not dismissed with political slogans. For me, acknowledging the pain does not mean rejecting the need for reform. It means asking how reform can be implemented more effectively and how people can be better protected through the transition. A policy can have a sound objective and still need adjustments. I want the government to listen, respond and improve what needs to work better. That is part of making reform succeed. We Should Acknowledge Meaningful Interventions: Alongside discussing the hardship, I believe we should recognise interventions intended to help people. NELFUND provides interest-free loans to help eligible students overcome financial barriers to higher education, with support for institutional fees and/or upkeep. These are loans with repayment obligations, not grants. For a student facing the possibility of leaving school because of money, access to financial support can make a meaningful difference. Education is one of the areas in which I want government intervention to open doors. MAMII is another initiative I welcome. It focuses on reducing maternal and newborn deaths through measures that include improving access to care, strengthening referral systems and helping services respond to complications during pregnancy and childbirth. As a country, we should care deeply about whether mothers can access care and whether students can continue their education. These programmes deserve attention, alongside honest questions about whom they are reaching, how effectively they are operating and what results they are delivering. I want them strengthened and delivered well. Recognising their value does not mean declaring the work complete. It means making room for a fair assessment of the administration. Accountability at Every Level: I expect leadership from the president. I also expect governors, local government chairmen, legislators and ministers to fulfil their responsibilities. Holding the presidency accountable should be the beginning of a wider demand for good governance, not the end of it. When communities lack functioning schools, healthcare, drainage or clean water, citizens should ask which institutions are responsible, what resources they have received and what they have delivered. We should ask these questions consistently, regardless of party affiliation. What is happening in our states? What is happening in our local governments? What are the people representing us doing with the responsibilities entrusted to them? I want this presidency to succeed, and I want every other level of government to do its part. Nigeria needs more than one office working. It needs public institutions and officials taking their responsibilities seriously. Public Money Must Deliver Public Value: Government must be able to explain what citizens’ sacrifices are achieving. Where revenues and allocations increase, people deserve to know how those resources are being used. How much was received? What was budgeted? What was spent? What was completed? And how has it improved people’s lives? These should be normal questions, not uncomfortable ones. I want to see public money translate into better schools, accessible healthcare, reliable infrastructure and essential services. I want clear reporting that allows citizens to judge performance beyond speeches and announcements. Public funds are not personal gifts from politicians. They are resources held in trust for the people. That trust must be respected at every level of government. Security Must Remain a Priority: Security is central to the Nigeria I want to see. Our farmers should be able to work without fear. Families should be able to travel safely. Communities should be protected, and businesses should be able to operate with confidence. These are not partisan expectations. They are basic expectations of government. I want the administration’s economic ambitions to be matched by sustained improvements in security. Progress must be felt in people’s confidence that they can travel, earn a living and go about their daily lives safely. That is an essential part of the success I want for this presidency. Support Should Not Require Blindness: I sometimes find our political culture exhausting. Apparently, you must either support everything a government does or oppose everything it does. There seems to be little room for thoughtful disagreement. I reject that thinking. I can support President Tinubu and question how a policy is being implemented. I can acknowledge progress and ask for greater urgency elsewhere. I can support the APC and still expect its public officials to explain their decisions and account for public resources. There is no contradiction in that. My questions do not come from uncertainty about where I stand. They come from wanting an administration I support to succeed. Loyalty should not mean silence. Criticism should not automatically mean opposition. We need room for honest conversations about what is working, what is not and what must happen next. That is the kind of political participation I believe in: committed, constructive and willing to speak honestly. Why I Support a Second Term: I want President Tinubu re-elected for a second term because I believe in his leadership and want him to complete the work he has begun. I believe continuity offers an opportunity to build on these reforms, improve their implementation and turn policy changes into improvements people can feel. That is my conviction, not a belief that time alone will solve our problems. Nigerians need relief today. People need affordable food, access to healthcare, reliable electricity, security and opportunities for their children. They need an economy in which hard work offers a reasonable chance of a decent living. Those expectations are fair, and I want this administration to meet them with greater urgency. For me, a second term should be an opportunity to build on what is working, correct what is not and deliver more widely. I want stronger businesses, functioning institutions, better infrastructure and genuine opportunities for young Nigerian

item.title: Why construction could become Africa’s key technology, investment opportunity
item.description: By Jimoh Razaq For years, Africa’s technology ecosystem has concentrated much of its entrepreneurial energy, investment capital and innovation around fintech, e-commerce, mobility, telecommunications and entertainment. These sectors have produced remarkable companies, attracted international investment and demonstrated that African businesses can build technology products capable of scaling across borders. But there is another industry with enormous economic significance, deeply entrenched inefficiencies and a largely untapped opportunity for technological transformation: construction. It is an industry that builds our homes, roads, hospitals, schools, factories, power infrastructure and cities. It employs millions of people, supports extensive manufacturing and distribution networks, moves significant volumes of capital and sits at the centre of economic development. Yet much of its operational infrastructure remains fragmented, manual and inefficient. While technology has transformed how people transfer money, order food, book transportation and access entertainment, the processes through which buildings and infrastructure are planned, financed, procured and delivered remain remarkably difficult to coordinate. This is not simply an operational inconvenience. It is a massive economic opportunity. The next generation of transformative African technology companies may emerge from solving the problems of the industries that physically build Africa. The industry technology has overlooked Construction is one of the world’s largest economic sectors. Global construction output was approximately $13 trillion in 2023, with projections suggesting it could reach $22 trillion by 2040. Yet its productivity performance remains disappointing. McKinsey’s 2024 research found that global construction productivity grew by approximately 0.4 per cent annually between 2000 and 2022, compared with around 2 per cent for the broader economy. This represents a productivity improvement of only about 10 per cent over more than two decades. The implications are significant. Projects experience delays. Budgets become unreliable. Material procurement remains fragmented. Labour productivity is difficult to measure. Project information is scattered across emails, spreadsheets, paper documents and messaging applications. Developers, contractors, consultants, suppliers, artisans and investors often operate without a shared information environment. item.content:encoded: By Jimoh Razaq For years, Africa’s technology ecosystem has concentrated much of its entrepreneurial energy, investment capital and innovation around fintech, e-commerce, mobility, telecommunications and entertainment. These sectors have produced remarkable companies, attracted international investment and demonstrated that African businesses can build technology products capable of scaling across borders. But there is another industry with enormous economic significance, deeply entrenched inefficiencies and a largely untapped opportunity for technological transformation: construction. It is an industry that builds our homes, roads, hospitals, schools, factories, power infrastructure and cities. It employs millions of people, supports extensive manufacturing and distribution networks, moves significant volumes of capital and sits at the centre of economic development. Yet much of its operational infrastructure remains fragmented, manual and inefficient. While technology has transformed how people transfer money, order food, book transportation and access entertainment, the processes through which buildings and infrastructure are planned, financed, procured and delivered remain remarkably difficult to coordinate. This is not simply an operational inconvenience. It is a massive economic opportunity. The next generation of transformative African technology companies may emerge from solving the problems of the industries that physically build Africa. The industry technology has overlooked Construction is one of the world’s largest economic sectors. Global construction output was approximately $13 trillion in 2023, with projections suggesting it could reach $22 trillion by 2040. Yet its productivity performance remains disappointing. McKinsey’s 2024 research found that global construction productivity grew by approximately 0.4 per cent annually between 2000 and 2022, compared with around 2 per cent for the broader economy. This represents a productivity improvement of only about 10 per cent over more than two decades. The implications are significant. Projects experience delays. Budgets become unreliable. Material procurement remains fragmented. Labour productivity is difficult to measure. Project information is scattered across emails, spreadsheets, paper documents and messaging applications. Developers, contractors, consultants, suppliers, artisans and investors often operate without a shared information environment. These challenges are particularly visible in emerging markets, where informal transactions, inconsistent data, financing constraints and infrastructure limitations compound existing industry inefficiencies. Africa’s infrastructure ambitions make the opportunity even more important. The OECD’s Africa’s Development Dynamics 2025 estimates that investing approximately $155 billion annually in infrastructure could significantly accelerate the continent’s economic growth. The question is not whether Africa needs more construction. It clearly does. The question is whether the industry can deliver the volume of housing, infrastructure and commercial development required without fundamentally changing how it operates. That is where technology founders should pay attention. Construction is not just an engineering industry. It is a technology ecosystem waiting to be connected. One of the biggest misconceptions about construction technology is that innovation is primarily about drones, robotics, 3D printing or sophisticated building design software. Those technologies matter, but they represent only a fraction of the opportunity. Construction is also an industry of financial transactions, procurement networks, logistics, labour coordination, data management, risk assessment, asset management and complex workflows. Every construction project creates multiple interconnected problems that technology can solve. Consider what happens when someone decides to build a house. They need to verify land ownership, develop architectural and structural drawings, estimate project costs, secure financing, identify qualified professionals, procure materials, engage artisans, manage construction activities, monitor expenditure and verify completion. Each stage involves multiple stakeholders, financial commitments and operational decisions. In many African markets, these activities are still managed through disconnected systems. There is an opportunity to build technology infrastructure that connects this entire process. Opportunities that could redefine construction in Africa AI-powered construction cost intelligence: One of the most persistent problems in construction is inaccurate project costing. Material prices fluctuate. Labour rates differ by location. Transportation costs change. Exchange-rate movements affect imported materials, while poor historical data makes reliable forecasting difficult. An intelligent construction cost engine could combine material prices, labour rates, geographical information, historical project costs and market conditions to generate more reliable estimates. Imagine a developer being able to estimate the cost of constructing a residential building in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan or Accra using current market information rather than relying entirely on outdated rate books. This is an opportunity for AI engineers, data scientists and construction professionals to build genuinely useful products. Digital construction material marketplaces: The procurement of cement, reinforcement steel, roofing materials, electrical fittings, plumbing components and other construction products remains highly fragmented. Buyers frequently depend on personal contacts, multiple quotations and informal supplier relationships. A verified digital marketplace could connect manufacturers, distributors, suppliers, contractors and developers through transparent pricing, product verification, digital payments and delivery tracking. Beyond convenience, such a platform could improve price discovery, reduce procurement fraud and create a more accountable supply chain. Save-To-Build financial technology: Millions of people want to build houses but cannot finance the entire project at once. Traditional construction financing is often inaccessible, while informal savings arrangements do not necessarily provide the structure or safeguards required for long-term building projects. A Save-To-Build platform could allow individuals to accumulate funds towards clearly defined construction milestones. For example, a customer could save towards land documentation, architectural design, foundation construction, roofing and finishing. Funds could be released against verified milestones, supported by appropriate financial safeguards and partnerships with regulated financial institutions. This creates an opportunity to connect personal finance, construction delivery and financial inclusion. AI-powered site supervision and project intelligence: Construction sites generate enormous amounts of information, but much of it is not systematically captured or analysed. Artificial intelligence, computer vision and mobile technology could help monitor construction progress, identify deviations from approved designs, track material consumption, record labour attendance and flag potential safety issues. A project owner could receive a digital site performance report without having to depend exclusively on periodic manual updates. The goal is not to replace professional site supervision or engineering judgement. It is to equip professionals with better information to make faster and more informed decisions. 5. Skilled labour and artisan marketplaces Africa’s construction industry depends heavily on skilled and semi-skilled workers, many of whom operate within informal employment networks. item.title: The future of automobile technology: Embracing AI for business growth in Nigeria
item.description: By Moses Stowe The growing importance of technological innovation, professional development and sustainable business growth in Nigeria’s automobile industry took centre stage at the 2026 Nigeria Automobile Technicians Association (NATA), Lagos State Council Day, where Intercontinental Distillers Limited (IDL), makers of Action Bitters, participated in an initiative recognising and supporting the contributions of automobile technicians to the nation’s economy. Held under the theme, “Harnessing Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Transform and Develop the Business of Auto Technicians in Nigeria,” this year’s celebration provided an important platform for industry stakeholders, automobile professionals, corporate organisations and association leaders to examine emerging opportunities in the automotive sector and the need to equip technicians with the knowledge, skills and resources required to remain competitive in an increasingly technology-driven industry. A major highlight of IDL’s participation was its support for the empowerment of automobile technicians through the provision of automobile tools. The initiative underscored the importance of practical support in strengthening the capacity of technicians, improving their operational efficiency and helping them deliver better services to customers. Beyond the recognition of their professional contributions, the gesture reflected the importance of providing tangible resources that can support the growth and sustainability of small businesses within the automobile value chain. Speaking on the significance of the occasion, Celestine Anyanwu, Brand Manager, Wine and Bitters, IDL, acknowledged the invaluable contributions of automobile technicians to the nation’s economic and industrial development. He noted that their expertise, dedication and entrepreneurial spirit remain essential to the effective functioning of the transportation and automobile sectors. He emphasised the importance of initiatives that recognise the efforts of professionals whose daily activities contribute to keeping businesses, individuals and transportation systems running. According to him, supporting the NATA community through the provision of relevant automobile tools represents a meaningful contribution towards professional development, business improvement and the advancement of the automobile servicing industry. He further acknowledged the relevance of this year’s theme, noting that Artificial Intelligence presents emerging opportunities for automobile technicians to improve diagnostic processes, embrace modern automotive technologies and develop more efficient approaches to business operations. He encouraged industry stakeholders to continue supporting platforms that promote innovation, practical empowerment and sustainable professional growth. A major highlight of IDL’s participation was its support for the empowerment of automobile technicians through the provision of automobile tools. Beyond the recognition of their professional contributions, the gesture reflected the importance of providing tangible resources that can support the growth and sustainability of small businesses within the automobile value chain. Speaking on the significance of the occasion, Celestine Anyanwu, Brand Manager, Wine and Bitters, IDL, acknowledged the invaluable contributions of automobile technicians to the nation’s economic and industrial development. He noted that their expertise, dedication and entrepreneurial spirit remain essential to the effective functioning of the transportation and automobile sectors. He emphasised the importance of initiatives that recognise the efforts of professionals whose daily activities contribute to keeping businesses, individuals and transportation systems running. According to him, supporting the NATA community through the provision of relevant automobile tools represents a meaningful contribution towards professional development, business improvement and the advancement of the automobile servicing industry. He further acknowledged the relevance of this year’s theme, noting that Artificial Intelligence presents emerging opportunities for automobile technicians to improve diagnostic processes, embrace modern automotive technologies and develop more efficient approaches to business operations. He encouraged industry stakeholders to continue supporting platforms that promote innovation, practical empowerment and sustainable professional growth. One of the major highlights of the event was the presentation of the grand prize, a complete set of automobile tool kits, to Kazeem Oladeji, one of the beneficiaries of the empowerment initiative. Expressing his appreciation, Oladeji described the award as a significant boost to his profession and business, noting that access to the right tools is essential to delivering quality automobile services. He commended Action Bitters and Intercontinental Distillers Limited for recognising the efforts of automobile technicians and extending support beyond mere celebration to practical empowerment. In the address of the Chairman of NATA, Lagos State Council, Morufu Egberongbe, described the celebration as a significant milestone in the association’s collective journey towards the growth, recognition, empowerment and professional development of automobile technicians across Lagos State and Nigeria. He reaffirmed the association’s commitment to promoting professionalism, unity, excellence and sustainable business development among its members, who operate across different segments of the automotive value chain. These include auto mechanics, auto electricians, panel beaters, spray painters, vulcanisers, auto air-conditioning technicians, diagnostic specialists, spare parts dealers and other related professionals. Egberongbe explained that the choice of this year’s theme reflected NATA’s determination to embrace innovation and adequately prepare its members for the future of the automotive industry. He noted that Artificial Intelligence and other emerging technologies are creating new possibilities for vehicle diagnostics, maintenance, customer service and business management, making continuous learning and adaptation increasingly important. The NATA chairman also expressed appreciation to corporate partners, sponsors and exhibitors for recognising the importance of the automobile technician community and supporting initiatives that promote innovation, capacity development and business growth. He described their contributions as investments in the future of the automotive industry and the thousands of businesses sustained by the sector. He equally acknowledged government institutions, industry leaders, association executives, the planning committee and other stakeholders whose contributions helped make the celebration a success. For IDL, its participation in the 2026 NATA Lagos State Council Day provided an opportunity to recognise a professional community whose contributions extend beyond automobile repairs to entrepreneurship, employment generation, technical expertise and economic development. The provision of automobile tools also highlighted an important dimension of corporate engagement: the need to support professional communities with resources that address practical business needs. For automobile technicians, access to appropriate tools is essential to improving service delivery, adapting to changing vehicle technologies and maintaining the confidence of customers. As Nigeria’s automotive landscape continues to evolve, the integration of Artificial Intelligence, digital diagnostic systems and modern vehicle maintenance solutions will increasingly shape the industry’s future. Platforms such as the NATA Lagos State Council Day therefore remain important in encouraging collaboration, knowledge exchange and stronger partnerships between professional associations and corporate stakeholders. Ultimately, the 2026 celebration reinforced a shared vision of an automobile industry built on technical competence, innovation, professional recognition and economic empowerment. Through its participation and support for the initiative, IDL joined other stakeholders in recognising the importance of strengthening the capabilities of automobile technicians and creating opportunities for the continued development of their businesses. The message was clear: the future of Nigeria’s automobile industry depends not only on technological advancement but also on empowering the skilled professionals who make the sector work. item.title: Oando’s rising fortunes: How Wale Tinubu is rewriting growth story
item.description: By Adebayo Adeoye Jubril Adewale Tinubu, CON, is not one to be easily satisfied with yesterday’s accomplishments. For the Oando Group Chief Executive, every milestone appears to present another opportunity to raise the bar, test new possibilities and push the boundaries of what an indigenous energy company can achieve. That restless ambition is once again finding expression in Oando’s improving fortunes. At Oando, the story has never been one of an overnight success. Rather, it is a tale of calculated risks, corporate reinvention and an unwavering belief in the possibilities of indigenous enterprise. Over the years, Tinubu has remained at the centre of the company’s evolution, steering its affairs through difficult economic seasons, industry uncertainties and the complex demands of a rapidly changing energy landscape. Today, the signs of another promising chapter are becoming increasingly visible, as the indigenous energy company continues to record encouraging improvements in its operations, strengthening its position in an industry where survival and relevance are often determined by the ability to anticipate change and respond decisively. For Tinubu, who has spent considerable years building Oando into a recognisable name in Africa’s energy industry, the latest developments represent more than a corporate milestone. They reflect an enduring ambition to build an indigenous institution capable of competing beyond Nigeria’s shores and holding its own among established players in the global energy market. One of the most encouraging aspects of Oando’s recent performance is the improvement in its operational efficiency. The company has continued to strengthen its production capacity, improve asset utilisation and address some of the operational challenges that have historically confronted the oil and gas industry. Its improving production profile suggests that the investments and management decisions taken over time are beginning to yield meaningful results. But beyond increased production, the company’s efforts to reduce operating costs and improve facility reliability have equally attracted attention. In an industry where operational disruptions can quickly erode profitability, efficiency remains a critical ingredient for sustainable growth. Oando’s renewed focus on operational discipline therefore speaks to a management philosophy that recognises the importance of building a business on solid foundations rather than merely pursuing expansion for its own sake. Indeed, Tinubu’s corporate journey has been defined by an appetite for ambitious decisions. His leadership at Oando has seen the company navigate major transitions, expand its interests and deepen its participation in Nigeria’s energy value chain. The acquisition of additional upstream assets further underscored his belief that indigenous companies should not remain spectators in an industry that has for decades been dominated by international oil companies. For the Oando Group Chief Executive, every milestone appears to present another opportunity to raise the bar, test new possibilities and push the boundaries of what an indigenous energy company can achieve. That restless ambition is once again finding expression in Oando’s improving fortunes. At Oando, the story has never been one of an overnight success. Rather, it is a tale of calculated risks, corporate reinvention and an unwavering belief in the possibilities of indigenous enterprise. Over the years, Tinubu has remained at the centre of the company’s evolution, steering its affairs through difficult economic seasons, industry uncertainties and the complex demands of a rapidly changing energy landscape. Today, the signs of another promising chapter are becoming increasingly visible, as the indigenous energy company continues to record encouraging improvements in its operations, strengthening its position in an industry where survival and relevance are often determined by the ability to anticipate change and respond decisively. For Tinubu, who has spent considerable years building Oando into a recognisable name in Africa’s energy industry, the latest developments represent more than a corporate milestone. They reflect an enduring ambition to build an indigenous institution capable of competing beyond Nigeria’s shores and holding its own among established players in the global energy market. One of the most encouraging aspects of Oando’s recent performance is the improvement in its operational efficiency. The company has continued to strengthen its production capacity, improve asset utilisation and address some of the operational challenges that have historically confronted the oil and gas industry. Its improving production profile suggests that the investments and management decisions taken over time are beginning to yield meaningful results. But beyond increased production, the company’s efforts to reduce operating costs and improve facility reliability have equally attracted attention. In an industry where operational disruptions can quickly erode profitability, efficiency remains a critical ingredient for sustainable growth. Oando’s renewed focus on operational discipline therefore speaks to a management philosophy that recognises the importance of building a business on solid foundations rather than merely pursuing expansion for its own sake. Indeed, Tinubu’s corporate journey has been defined by an appetite for ambitious decisions. His leadership at Oando has seen the company navigate major transitions, expand its interests and deepen its participation in Nigeria’s energy value chain. The acquisition of additional upstream assets further underscored his belief that indigenous companies should not remain spectators in an industry that has for decades been dominated by international oil companies. That ambition, however, comes with its own demands. The acquisition and development of oil and gas assets require substantial capital, careful financial management and the ability to balance immediate obligations with long-term business objectives. Oando is not insulated from these pressures, particularly as it continues to manage the financial commitments associated with its expansion strategy. Nevertheless, the company’s improving operating performance offers reasons for optimism. Its ability to generate cash from operations while maintaining investments in drilling and other production-related activities demonstrates a determination to sustain its growth trajectory. Equally important is the company’s continuing effort to strengthen its financial position and manage its borrowing obligations. For Tinubu, the task is clearly not simply to preserve what has already been built but to ensure that Oando remains relevant in an industry undergoing profound transformation. The global conversation around energy security, cleaner energy sources and sustainable development is changing the rules of engagement. Indigenous energy companies must therefore demonstrate not only financial resilience but also the capacity to adapt to emerging realities. This is where the Oando story becomes particularly interesting. Tinubu has consistently projected the ambition of an African entrepreneur who believes that local businesses can rise above structural limitations and compete on a much bigger stage. His approach has been characterised by bold corporate moves, strategic partnerships and an understanding that the future belongs to companies willing to evolve. Yet, beyond the boardroom calculations and corporate announcements, there is also the question of legacy. Building a successful company is one thing; establishing an institution that can withstand changing leadership, economic cycles and industry disruptions is another. It is a challenge that every ambitious business leader must eventually confront. For now, Oando appears determined to keep its place in the unfolding energy narrative. Its improving operational fortunes provide fresh momentum, while Tinubu’s leadership continues to attract attention as the company pursues its broader ambitions. Clearly, the Oando story is far from finished. And if the current momentum is anything to go by, Wale Tinubu is not ready to take his foot off the accelerator. In the competitive race for relevance in Africa’s energy industry, he appears determined to ensure that Oando is not merely present at the table but has a voice in deciding where the industry goes. Adeoye Adebayo writes in from Lagos. The post Oando’s rising fortunes: How Wale Tinubu is rewriting growth story appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: 2027: Imperative of Peter Mbah’s second term in Enugu
item.description: By Willy Eya Politics apart, Enugu State Governor, Dr Peter Mbah deserves a second term in office. That is not contestable. Certainly, the governor’s achievements since assumption of office in 2023 will campaign for him ahead of the 2027 general elections. One good turn, they say, deserves another. Mbah came in as an accomplished technocrat determined to reshape the public sector using his private sector background.He approaches governance with a structured blueprint rather than the usual, impromptu trial-and-error tactics by regular Nigerian politicians. Every step the governor takes is intentional, hence, he links infrastructure directly to economic growth. His idea for instance is that fixing roads or investing heavily in security isn’t just for safety but a targeted prerequisite to open up the state for tourism, agriculture, and private sector investments. He deliberately avoided slow, conventional governance steps and pushed instead for immediate macro-level structural adjustments from Day One.Mbah’s strength lies in translating private-sector efficiency into public-sector execution.This quality is evidenced by his courage to dismantle slow legacy systems—such as implementing the fully digitized Enugu Geographic Information Service (ENGIS) to fast-track land administration and heavily relying on data to drive executive decisions. Unlike career politicians who rely on political patronage, the governor is largely a corporate technocrat whose leadership is rooted in rigorous planning. From inception after his inauguration, he was clear in his road-map to radically change the story of Enugu State. His first major challenge was to end the Monday Sit-at-Home disruptions. For years, the illegal “sit-at-home” orders crippled the economy of the Southeast and his immediate and uncompromising ban on the orders from his first week in office is frequently cited as a defining test of his leadership.Despite initial hiccups, the administration restored normal business and economic activities on Mondays and Enugu State is better for it today. In his cabinet appointments, Mbah consciously shifted the political culture of Enugu State by actively recruiting top-tier professionals from academia and the global private sector. He believes in inclusive and merit-based governance, hence, prioritized competence over partisan rewards.
